batch.h2: Batch moves big data in chunks, and remembers where it stopped.
batch.sub: Think of importing a 5-million-row CSV. One giant <term k="transaction">transaction</term> would run out of memory and lose everything on the first bad row. Batch reads and processes items one at a time, writes them in small chunks, and records progress in database tables so a failed job can resume.
batch.items0: Every chunk runs the same loop: read one item, process it, repeat until the chunk is full, then write them all together. Pick a trail to zoom in on one worker. The chunk size here is 2 so the whole loop fits on screen.
batch.items1: Reader, processor and writer, step by step
batch.items2: The reader has the smallest contract of the three: return the next item, or null when there is nothing left. Everything else is its own business: opening the file, buffering, paging, and remembering how far it got.
batch.items3: The interface, and a CSV reader
batch.items5: A reader keeps a cursor, so one instance must not be shared between threads unless it is built for that. Database readers come in a restart-safe paging flavour and a faster single-thread cursor flavour.
batch.items6: Its name is how restart works
batch.items7: On commit the reader writes its position into the ExecutionContext under its name. Without a stable name there is nothing to find on restart, and a failed job would begin at record 1 again.
batch.items9: The processor sees one item at a time and returns something for the writer. It is optional, but it is the right home for cleaning, converting, validating and deciding to skip. It has exactly three possible outcomes.
batch.items10: A processor that cleans, filters and validates
batch.items17: Adds it to the chunk for the writer
batch.items21: Drops the item quietly, no error
batch.items25: Fails the step, or skips or retries it if you configured that
batch.items27: Keep processors free of slow work. Calling a remote API for every item is the most common reason an import crawls. Preload a lookup table, or batch the calls in the writer instead.
batch.items28: ItemProcessor: where your business rules live
batch.items29: The writer is called once per chunk, never once per item, and receives every processed item as a single list. That is what makes batch inserts, bulk API calls and single file flushes possible.
batch.items30: The interface, and a JDBC batch writer
batch.items32: A database writer runs inside the chunk transaction, so a failure <term k="rollback">rolls back</term> every row of the chunk together. That is also why a bad row can cost a whole chunk.
batch.items34: A writer that sends emails or calls a REST API cannot be rolled back. If the chunk is retried, those effects can happen twice, so make them safe to repeat, for example with an idempotency key.
batch.items35: ItemWriter: the whole chunk at once
batch.items36: Most jobs combine ready-made classes. You write the processor, and sometimes nothing else.
batch.items44: Skips header lines, maps columns to a type
batch.items47: A database, one page at a time

tools.h2: Lombok and MapStruct write the repetitive Java for you, at compile time.

Both work while the project compiles, so the generated code is plain Java at runtime.

0.q: Who creates the OrderService instance in a Spring application?
0.w: Spring scans for components at startup and creates each bean once, in dependency order.

1.q: What does component scan look for?
1.o0: Classes annotated with @Component or a stereotype that includes it
1.o2: Only classes whose name ends in Service
1.w: @Service, @Repository and @RestController all contain @Component, so scanning finds them.

2.q: Why must a bean's dependencies be created before the bean itself?
2.o1: Its constructor arguments must already exist
2.w: Constructor injection needs real objects to pass in, so Spring builds the dependency graph and creates leaves first.

0.q: Which injection style allows the field to be final?
0.w: A final field must be assigned in the constructor. Field and setter injection assign it later.

1.q: Two beans implement PaymentClient and nothing else is configured. What happens at startup?
1.o0: The first one alphabetically is used
1.w: Spring refuses to guess. Add @Primary or use @Qualifier to choose.

2.q: What does @RequiredArgsConstructor put in the generated constructor?
2.o1: Final fields with no value, and @NonNull fields
2.w: Non-final fields are skipped, which is why services keep their dependencies final.

0.q: What is the difference in behaviour between @Service and @Component?
0.o2: @Service is a singleton and @Component is not
0.w: Both create the same kind of bean. The stereotype tells readers which layer a class belongs to.

1.q: When does a @PostConstruct method run?
1.o1: After injection, before the proxy exists
1.w: That is why calling a @Transactional method from @PostConstruct runs without a transaction.

2.q: What is the default scope of a bean?
2.w: One shared instance per container, so beans should not keep per-request data in fields.

0.q: What is a starter?
0.o0: A class that starts the server
0.o1: A dependency that pulls in a set of libraries Boot can configure
0.w: A starter is just a dependency. Boot then checks the classpath and creates matching beans.

1.q: Your own @Bean and an auto-configured bean have the same type. Which one is used?
1.w: Auto-configuration backs off when you define your own bean.

2.q: Which component picks the controller method for a request?
2.w: The DispatcherServlet is the front controller. HandlerMapping holds the routing table built from your annotations.

0.q: A command-line argument and application.yml set the same property. Which wins?
0.w: The command line is near the top of the priority list, so it overrides files.

1.q: What does @ConfigurationProperties give you over @Value?
1.w: One record holds a whole group of settings, with type conversion and validation.

2.q: How do you activate the prod profile?
2.w: Set it as a property, a command-line flag or the SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE environment variable.

0.q: Why return a DTO instead of the entity?
0.o1: To control exactly which fields leave the API
0.w: A DTO keeps internal fields such as password hashes and lazy relations out of the response.

1.q: A POST body has a blank email, with @Valid and @NotBlank. What does the client get?
1.w: Validation fails before your method is called, and a handler turns it into a 400.

2.q: Which annotation reads a value from the query string?
2.w: @PathVariable reads the URL path, @RequestParam reads ?name=value, and @RequestBody reads the body.

0.q: Where do you put an @ExceptionHandler that applies to every controller?
0.w: @RestControllerAdvice is shared by all controllers.

1.q: Which status fits a customer that does not exist?
1.w: 404 means the resource was not found. 409 is for a conflict with current state.

2.q: Why not return the exception message and stack trace to clients?
2.o1: It can leak internals to attackers
2.w: Log the details on the server and send a generic message.

0.q: Which interface groups the rows of a join into nested objects?
0.w: A ResultSetExtractor receives the whole ResultSet, so you can group rows yourself.

1.q: What does @Param("email") do?
1.o1: Binds the method argument to :email in the query
1.w: The name in @Param must match the named placeholder in the query text.

2.q: What is the main benefit of an interface projection?
2.o0: It selects only the columns you need
2.w: Spring Data reads only the properties the interface declares.

0.q: You load a Customer in a transaction and call setFirstName without save(). What happens at commit?
0.o1: Hibernate detects the change and issues an UPDATE
0.o3: The change stays in the cache only
0.w: Dirty checking compares the managed entity with its snapshot at flush time.

1.q: You loop over 100 customers and call getOrders() on each lazily. How many queries run?
1.w: One query for the customers plus one per customer: the N+1 problem.

2.q: What causes LazyInitializationException?
2.o0: Reading a lazy relation after the session or transaction closed
2.w: The entity is detached, so there is no open session to load the relation.

0.q: A @Transactional method throws a checked IOException. By default, what happens?
0.w: Spring rolls back only for RuntimeException and Error unless you set rollbackFor.

1.q: A @Transactional method is called from another method in the same class. What happens?
1.w: The call never goes through the proxy, so no transaction is started.

2.q: What does REQUIRES_NEW do?
2.o1: Suspends the current one and starts an independent one
2.w: The inner work commits or rolls back on its own.

0.q: Which annotation starts only the web layer?
0.w: @WebMvcTest loads controllers, JSON conversion and validation, but not services or repositories.

1.q: Why do @DataJpaTest tests roll back by default?
1.o0: To leave the database clean between tests
1.w: Each test runs in a transaction that is rolled back, so tests do not affect each other.

2.q: In a @WebMvcTest the controller needs CustomerService. What do you do?
2.w: The web slice does not load services, so you supply a mock.

0.q: A request has a valid token but lacks the required role. Which status does it get?
0.w: 401 means unknown caller. 403 means known caller, not allowed.

1.q: Which flow suits a single-page app that logs users in through an external provider?
1.w: PKCE replaces the client secret that a public client cannot keep.

2.q: Why does the client secret belong on a server, not in a browser app?
2.o0: A browser app cannot keep a secret
2.w: Anything shipped to the browser can be read by the user.

0.q: Record 7 fails in a chunk of 5 (records 6 to 10). Which rows are committed?
0.o0: Only earlier chunks, so records 1 to 5
0.w: The failing chunk rolls back as a whole. Earlier chunks were already committed.

1.q: What lets a failed job restart where it stopped?
1.w: Batch stores execution state and the last committed position in its tables.

2.q: What does returning null from an ItemProcessor do?
2.w: The item is skipped without error and counted in the filter count.

3.q: How many items does ItemWriter.write receive per call?
3.o0: The whole chunk, as one list
3.o3: Two: the current and the previous
3.w: The writer runs once per chunk, which is what allows batch inserts and one commit per chunk.

4.q: Where should per-item business logic, such as cleaning an email, go?
4.w: The processor sees one item at a time, can transform or filter it, and keeps the reader and writer simple.

0.q: On the second call with the same arguments, a @Cacheable method...
0.o1: returns the stored value without running
0.w: The proxy answers from the cache and skips the real method.

1.q: You call an @Async method from another method in the same class. What happens?
1.o1: It runs synchronously, because the proxy is bypassed
1.w: Same rule as @Transactional: self-calls skip the proxy.

2.q: Two copies of the application run. What happens to a @Scheduled job?
2.o0: It runs once for the cluster
2.o3: It runs on the first only
2.w: Each instance has its own scheduler. Use a shared lock if the job must run once.

0.q: When does Lombok generate its code?
0.w: Lombok edits the class inside javac, so the .class file already contains the generated methods.

1.q: Why avoid @Data on JPA entities?
1.o1: equals, hashCode and toString can touch lazy relations
1.w: Those methods may load lazy collections or loop through bidirectional relationships.

2.q: What does @Mapper(componentModel = "spring") add?
2.o0: A Spring bean you can inject
2.w: The generated implementation is annotated as a component.

0.q: Which pattern explains why @Transactional works through a wrapper?
0.w: Spring gives callers a proxy that adds behaviour before and after your method.

1.q: Which pattern does the DispatcherServlet implement?
1.w: One entry point decides which handler runs.

2.q: JdbcTemplate fixes the skeleton and you supply one part. Which pattern is that?
2.w: The fixed algorithm calls your callback at the variable step.

0.q: Where does the 400 for an invalid body come from?
0.o1: MethodArgumentNotValidException, handled before the service runs
0.w: Validation fails at the controller boundary, and the advice class builds the response.

1.q: At which step does the transaction open?
1.o1: When the proxy calls the @Transactional service method
1.w: The proxy begins the transaction before the method body and commits after it returns.

2.q: Why does the controller return OrderResponse and not Order?
2.o1: The entity stays inside; only chosen fields leave
2.w: A response DTO controls exactly what the client sees.

0.q: Startup fails with NoSuchBeanDefinitionException for PaymentClient. What is the most likely cause?
0.o0: PaymentClient is not a bean: no annotation, or outside the scanned package
0.o2: The port is already in use
0.w: Spring only creates beans it finds by scanning or through @Bean methods.

1.q: In a long stack trace, which line usually names the real problem?
1.w: Wrapper exceptions come first. The root cause is the last Caused by at the bottom.

2.q: A controller throws LazyInitializationException. What is a good fix?
2.o0: Load the data inside the service transaction, or return a DTO
2.w: The session is closed once the service returns, so the data must be loaded before that point.

0.q: Where does springdoc get its description of your endpoints?
0.o0: From your controllers and their types, read at runtime
0.o1: From a YAML file you maintain
0.w: It scans the mappings, parameters and return types, then builds the OpenAPI document.

1.q: What does Spring Data REST need in order to expose /customers?
1.w: It generates the controller itself from the repository.

2.q: Which URL serves the raw OpenAPI JSON by default with springdoc?
2.w: Swagger UI reads this same document and draws the interactive page from it.

0.q: In Express you write app.use(logger). What is the closest Spring idea?
0.o0: A servlet filter or an interceptor
0.w: Both run code around every request before it reaches your handler.

1.q: What plays the role of package.json dependencies in a Spring Boot project?
1.w: Maven or Gradle resolves and downloads the libraries.

2.q: Which file plays the role of .env and settings files?
2.w: Ports, database URLs and feature flags live there, with one file per profile.

0.q: What does joinPoint.proceed() do in @Around advice?
0.o0: Runs the real method, or the next advice
0.w: The advice decides when, and whether, the real method runs. Without proceed() it never executes.

1.q: Which question does a pointcut expression answer?
1.o0: Which methods should the advice apply to?
1.w: A pointcut selects join points, which in Spring AOP are method calls on beans.

2.q: Why does a method calling this.audit() skip the aspect?
2.o0: The call does not go through the proxy
2.o1: Aspects only work on public fields
2.o3: AOP is switched off in tests
2.w: this is the real object. Only calls that arrive through the proxy can be intercepted.

bean.d: An object that Spring creates, keeps and hands out. Any class Spring manages is a bean.

component.d: A class marked so Spring finds it while scanning, with @Component or a stereotype such as @Service.

di.d: A class asks for the helpers it needs and something else hands them over, instead of the class creating them itself.

context.d: The container. It creates the beans, wires them together and shuts them down.

proxy.d: A generated stand-in that wraps a bean to add behaviour such as transactions, caching or logging.

stereotype.d: An annotation such as @Service or @Repository that marks a class as a bean and says which layer it belongs to.

singleton.d: One shared instance for the whole container. It is the default scope of a bean.

aspect.d: A class that holds behaviour needed by many methods, such as logging or timing, written once instead of repeated.

advice.d: The code an aspect runs at a chosen point: before, after or around a method.

pointcut.d: An expression that selects which methods an aspect applies to.

joinpoint.d: A moment where advice can run. In Spring AOP it is always a method call.

transaction.d: A group of database changes that succeed or fail together.

rollback.d: Undoing every change made since the transaction began.

dto.d: Data Transfer Object: a plain class that defines exactly what goes into or out of an API.

projection.d: Reading only some columns into a smaller type instead of loading the whole entity.

dirty.d: Hibernate noticing that a loaded entity changed and writing the UPDATE at commit without being asked.

chunk.d: A fixed-size group of items that a batch step reads, processes, writes and commits together.

filterchain.d: An ordered list of filters every request passes through before it reaches your controller.

jwt.d: JSON Web Token: a signed token that carries the user's identity, so the server needs no session.

oauth.d: A standard that lets an app act for a user without ever seeing their password.

cors.d: A browser rule that stops a page calling another origin unless that server allows it.

csrf.d: An attack where another site makes your browser send a request you did not intend, using your logged-in session.

starter.d: A dependency that pulls in a ready-made set of libraries for one purpose, such as web or JPA.

autoconfig.d: Boot creating beans for you when it finds the matching libraries on the classpath.

profile.d: A named set of configuration, such as dev or prod, switched on when the application starts.

lombok.d: A compile-time tool that generates boilerplate such as getters and constructors from annotations.

mapstruct.d: A compile-time tool that generates the code that maps one class to another.
